ph7-7-the-adi-granth.html:
The Adi Granth

In 1604 Guru Arjan oversaw the compilation of the Adi Granth and its installation at Harmandir Sahib. Its musical organisation and selected contributors are important features. The book can be described accurately without a competitive claim that no other scripture has ever done anything comparable.

7.1 — Why compile at all

Compilation served the preservation and organisation of the teaching. Rival claims and competing compositions formed part of the setting. They should not be presented as the sole proved motive for a decision with a larger religious and institutional significance.

Guru Arjan's elder brother Prithi Chand had been passed over for the succession and did not accept it. He and his followers established a rival claim — and, importantly, circulated their own compositions, some written to resemble those of the Gurus.

For a community receiving teaching through verse, attribution matters. An authoritative compilation helps readers distinguish the accepted corpus from other compositions, while manuscript history remains a separate field of investigation. Authority is not the same as pretending that every copying question has disappeared.

The compilation gathered and ordered an accepted body of material. Calling it authoritative describes its religious reception. To describe the exact production and transmission of a particular surviving manuscript, the reader must still examine that manuscript, its evidence of date and the scholarship concerning it.

7.2 — How it was done

Guru Arjan gathered the collections that had been passed down from Guru Angad and Guru Amar Das, together with material sought out from elsewhere, and worked through them.

Bhai Gurdas is remembered as the scribe in the compilation under Guru Arjan. Ramsar at Amritsar and the year 1604 belong to the established account of that compilation. These details concern the Adi Granth stage, not a claim that the present received corpus was already identical in every respect.

The finished volume was installed in the Harmandir Sahib, and Baba Buddha — an elderly follower who had known Guru Nanak himself — was appointed its first attendant.

Hold that last detail for a moment.

The man appointed to look after the completed scripture in 1604 had, as a young man, met Nanak.

Baba Buddha occupies an important place in Sikh memory of the early Gurus. Accounts of his participation connect generations of the community. Such a biographical tradition should be identified as such, rather than used as independent verification of every scene described across that period.

7.3 — Arranged by music

The musical organisation is worth noticing because it shapes how readers find and receive compositions. It is a feature of this scripture, not a reason to claim that no other religious literature has musical arrangements.

Most of the corpus is arranged in raag sections, with further organisation by authorship and compositional form. Opening and concluding materials require their own descriptions. Saying that the whole book is organised only by music would omit those features and make the reader expect a simpler structure than the book actually has.

Raga: a melodic framework in Indian classical music — a set of notes with rules about how they move, associated with a particular mood and often a time of day or season.

Within raag sections, headings, authorial designations and forms help organise the compositions. A reader should notice all of them. The heading Mahalla, for example, is not a decoration to ignore because a familiar name appears elsewhere in the shabad.

Musical location is one important part of a hymn's address. Authorial heading and compositional context are also important. A useful citation lets a reader find the same passage and understand why it has been identified in that way.

Why does the arrangement matter?

The arrangement gives singing and congregation a substantial place in receiving the teaching. It does not prohibit study, interpretation or commentary. A scripture can be sung and examined carefully; those activities need not be treated as rivals.

Musicians and congregations are central to this reception, alongside teachers, interpreters and individual readers. The musical form does not make thought unnecessary. It provides one way in which the teaching is encountered and remembered.

The inclusion of bhagat compositions in the received canon deserves attention on its own terms. Their location alongside the Gurus' compositions expresses an editorial and religious recognition. It need not be justified by a theory that every book arranged by author must inevitably create an unjust hierarchy.

7.4 — Who is in it

The scripture contains the compositions of the Gurus. It also contains the work of a group of earlier and contemporary devotional poets — the bhagats — and of several musicians and court poets attached to the Gurus.

Look at who the bhagats are, by background:

The corpus also contains bhatt compositions and other attributed material. Rubrics associated with musicians, including Mardana, require precise reading; the appearance of a name is not automatically a simple modern author list. The contributor backgrounds in the table are conventional biographical identifications, with several details preserved through tradition rather than independently verified personal records.

A statement that truth has no owner

Including compositions attributed to figures from different social and religious backgrounds is a substantial feature of the canon. The religious significance lies in the compositions received as teaching, not in making the whole outside tradition of each contributor interchangeable with Sikh doctrine. A selected voice is not a declaration that every other work or practice associated with that voice is approved.

A careful and selective act, not an open door

The compilation was selective. Inclusion and selection should be held together: recognised compositions from a broader devotional landscape were received within a particular canon. Neither the contributor's background alone nor a modern label attached to it can replace reading what the selected composition actually says.

We tend to treat scriptures as things that simply exist — received, complete, without a history of assembly.

The assumption is that a scripture is found rather than made.

What this chapter shows is the opposite, and shows it unusually clearly because the process is documented. Someone gathered material. Someone decided what was genuine and what was not. Someone chose an arrangement. Someone chose which outside voices to admit. Someone wrote it down, and someone installed it.

Scriptures have different histories of composition and collection. This chapter concerns the identifiable compilation under Guru Arjan. It does not claim to have surveyed every scripture's formation. Naming a compiler and scribe is useful evidence, while particular decisions and manuscript details can still require investigation.

Acknowledging compilation is compatible with reverence for the scripture. It identifies work undertaken to preserve and organise a corpus. A reason sometimes offered for that work, such as concern about rival compositions, should be presented with its supporting tradition rather than converted into an exclusive explanation for every editorial decision.

The Adi Granth was compiled by Guru Arjan with Bhai Gurdas as scribe, completed in 1604, and installed in the Harmandir Sahib.

Rival compositions form part of the context in which Sikh tradition describes compilation. Preservation, religious authority and organisation also matter. A reader should not reduce the book to an emergency response to one family dispute.

Raag sections play a major role in organising the corpus, together with headings, authorship and forms. Opening and concluding materials have their own organisation. Reading the actual page is better than relying on an absolute slogan about the entire arrangement.

The canon includes bhagat compositions associated with varied backgrounds. The table gives conventional biographical descriptions, not proof that every detail of every contributor's life is settled. Their inclusion is worth understanding without a claim of superiority over all other scriptures.

The memory of Baba Buddha connects the generations of the early community. Read it as an important biographical tradition and distinguish it from the manuscript evidence for a particular surviving volume.

ph7-5-gurmukhi-a-script-of-ones-own.html:
Gurmukhi: A Script of One's Own

Punjabi could be written before Guru Angad. Gurmukhi developed within an existing regional world of scripts rather than arriving from nowhere. Its standardisation and its place in Sikh transmission are substantial achievements without the false claim that the population previously possessed no usable writing at all.

5.1 — The situation before

Different languages and scripts held different kinds of prestige. Persian was important in administration; Arabic in Islamic learning; Sanskrit in several learned and religious traditions. Local vernaculars and writing practices also existed. The following overview is simplified and should not be read as an exclusive assignment of one language to every person or activity.

  • Persian — government, law, revenue, courts, high poetry. Written in Arabic script.
  • Arabic — Islamic scripture and scholarship.
  • Sanskrit — Hindu learning and ritual, written in Devanagari or local variants.
  • Punjabi — a widely spoken vernacular with regional writing practices; its relation to literary and administrative use changed over time.

Commercial scripts and regional writing practices predated Gurmukhi's standardisation. Some abbreviated writing relies heavily on the reader's knowledge, but not all earlier writing was incapable of recording a complete text. The historical question concerns development and use, not a universal verdict that every older script failed.

5.2 — What Gurmukhi is

Gurmukhi was developed and standardised under Guru Angad out of those existing local scripts, which trace back through a chain to the ancient Brahmi of Part 4.

The name is usually understood as "from the mouth of the Guru".

Guru Angad is credited with standardising and promoting Gurmukhi. Its letters and vowel signs support the recording and teaching of the corpus. No script is entirely free of questions about pronunciation, interpretation or historical spelling; standardisation makes a shared practice more available rather than abolishing every ambiguity.

An everyday analogy can help explain standardisation, provided it is not mistaken for a complete account of the earlier scripts. A private abbreviated note and a text intended for unfamiliar readers place different demands on writing.

A shorthand works when the reader already knows roughly what it says. Write 4 bgs wht, Rm and a merchant who was expecting it will understand.

Now try using that system for a hymn that must be sung correctly, in the right words, in a village a hundred kilometres away, by someone who has never heard it.

If crucial information is omitted, an unfamiliar reader may struggle to recover it. Clear conventions can help. This illustrates one function of a shared script; it does not prove that every prior system failed immediately or that one new script makes every reading identical.

Accurate transmission is one important benefit of standardisation. The exact intentions behind each historical development should not be asserted as though a signed design brief survives. Religious, educational and social uses can grow together rather than having one exclusive technical cause.

5.3 — Why a script is never just a script

The assumption is that a script is a neutral tool — a way of recording sounds, with no meaning of its own.

A script can carry social associations as well as recording language. Those associations vary with users, institutions and history; they are not a fixed law determining every person's access.

A script determines who can read what, and therefore who has access to knowledge. It carries the prestige of whatever is already written in it. And it marks a text as belonging to one world rather than another.

Consider what the alternatives would have meant for Nanak's hymns.

Written in Arabic script: they would have sat visually alongside Persian government documents and Islamic religious texts, and been read by the class educated in those.

Written in Devanagari: they would have sat alongside Sanskrit scripture, and been read by the class educated in that.

Gurmukhi became closely associated with Sikh scripture and learning. Its regional antecedents mean it did not stand outside all existing literacy. Its association with an identifiable community helped give it a durable institutional role.

Learning letters opens a useful door, but it is not the same as understanding historical vocabulary, grammar, metaphor and musical forms. Teachers and explanations can help without becoming owners of the teaching. Promoting literacy and permitting interpretation are compatible aims.

An accessible script can reduce some barriers to participation. It does not automatically remove every social gatekeeper or guarantee universal literacy. The achievement should be described in terms of actual teaching, copying and reading rather than a claim that control vanished at once.

5.4 — Punjab's third writing system

It helps to distinguish a script's ancestry from its later institutional life. Continuity in letter forms is not the same question as continuity in the communities teaching and using them.

The much older Indus signs remain undeciphered. They should not be presented as a known ancestral Sikh language or as a system whose meaning has been recovered. A similarity in the region where objects were found does not establish a continuous religious tradition.

Other historical scripts, including Kharosthi and Brahmi-derived regional forms, belong to the wider history of writing in and around Punjab. Counting Gurmukhi as the region's literal third script would erase other writing systems and confuse different historical categories.

Gurmukhi is a living script with a significant place in Sikh and Punjabi life. Its survival can be explained through continued teaching and use without a numbered contest between supposedly only three scripts.

When a writing system stops being taught, access to its texts can narrow or disappear. That is a useful general observation. It does not mean that all texts in every older regional script are either wholly lost or impossible to read today.

The script associated with Guru Angad's standardisation remains in use in education, publishing, public communication and scripture. That living use is the achievement to describe; a claim that it began without antecedents is unnecessary.

Institutions that teach a script contribute to its survival. Communities, schools, publishing, administration and changing political circumstances can all matter. One cause should not be declared the exact and exclusive explanation for the fate of every other script.

Earlier Punjabi writing existed. Gurmukhi developed and was standardised within that regional history. The important distinction is between claiming invention from nothing and recognising development, promotion and a lasting place in transmission.

A shared set of letter and vowel conventions supports reading and copying. It does not make historical language automatically transparent or eliminate every interpretive question.

Transmission, education and religious identity are relevant to the script's history. An exact statement of intention requires its own evidence; the benefit of a development is not always a complete explanation of its original motive.

A person can learn the script and begin studying directly. Understanding can still require explanation, practice and attention to context. Access is increased by useful teaching, not by promising that a short alphabet lesson makes every passage self-explanatory.

The wider region has a long history of writing systems. Gurmukhi's continuing life is worth understanding within that history, without reducing the entire record to three systems.

ph8-9-1708-ending-the-line.html:
1708: Ending the Line

The death of Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded in 1708 and the transfer of Guruship are central to Sikh tradition. The development changed the location of recognised authority; it did not permanently eliminate every dispute about leadership, interpretation or the institutions of the Panth.

9.1 — Nanded

In 1708 Guru Gobind Singh was at Nanded, on the Godavari in the Deccan, having travelled south with Bahadur Shah's camp.

Accounts describe the Guru being attacked and dying after treatment of the wound. They connect the attack with Wazir Khan. The conventional date of death is 7 October 1708. Particular details of the attack and treatment should be traced to their sources rather than treated as equally documented eyewitness observations.

9.2 — What he did before he died

He declared that the line of human Gurus was ended, and that authority would pass to two things.

Sikh tradition recognises the Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru following the tenth Guru. The received corpus includes Guru Tegh Bahadur's compositions. The 1604 compilation and the subsequent history of the received text must be distinguished rather than collapsed into one unchanged stage.

The tradition also recognises the Panth's collective responsibility and authority. How that authority is exercised, who participates and which institution represents it are questions with a later history, not matters settled by simply repeating the phrase Guru Panth.

Guru Granth: the scripture as eternal Guru. Consulted for guidance; treated with the honours given to a living Guru.

Guru Panth: the community as Guru. In practice, decisions taken by an assembly of initiated Sikhs — a Gurmata — carry the authority of the Guru.

He also, according to the tradition, commissioned a man he had met at Nanded — an ascetic who took the name Banda Singh Bahadur — and sent him north to Punjab with a small band and written orders.

Banda Singh Bahadur's subsequent campaigns are discussed in Part 9 of this Sikhism series. Their significance includes the practical challenge of leadership and mobilisation after the tenth Guru's death.

9.3 — What problem this solved

Look at the record of the previous century and the problem becomes obvious.

Several successions had produced rival claims, including those associated with Prithi Chand, Ram Rai and claimants at Bakala. That record supports discussion of recurring contestation, not the absolute statement that every single succession had been contested in the same way.

Some Gurus faced imperial execution and others assumed Guruship while young. These facts help explain why questions about continuity and authority mattered. They do not establish that the earlier community could be wholly destroyed by removing one individual.

A line of human Gurus is therefore two vulnerabilities in one: it can be disputed from inside and removed from outside.

Recognising a scripture as Guru changes the form of authority. It does not prevent disputes about manuscripts, interpretation or institutional decisions. A widely copied text provides resources for checking, but copying and religious recognition are not magical guarantees that no altered copy can ever exist.

Collective responsibility can make a community less dependent on a single successor. Communities still remain vulnerable to persecution and their institutions need leadership and organisation. The requirement to keep a kirpan is not proof that every initiated member in every place is identically armed, trained or able to fight.

The eighteenth-century community survived severe attacks through mobilisation and adaptation. The transfer of Guruship is part of that history. Survival should not be explained by one mechanism while ignoring people, resources, local conditions and changing alliances.

Underneath most thinking about religious institutions sits an assumption so ordinary it is invisible:

That authority has to live in a person.

Look at the alternatives available in 1708 and what each would have meant.

Another personal succession would have raised questions about recognition and continuity. This is an analytical comparison, not a claim to have access to the tenth Guru's private deliberations about every hypothetical alternative.

An inherited religious office would have raised different questions about the relation between household, teaching and authority. The comparison helps a reader think, but it does not prove that every later teacher or official is a forbidden intermediary.

A council also depends on people, procedures and accountability. It can be disrupted or contested. That practical vulnerability is not unique to councils, and it does not mean that collective institutions are inherently pointless.

Scripture and collective responsibility provide a different arrangement. Their authority does not remove the human work of preservation, interpretation and decision. People still need to decide how a collective judgment is reached and how a claimed representative is held accountable.

The development challenges the assumption that the same kind of personal successor must continue indefinitely. It does not establish that nobody is in charge of any later institution, or that the community has no need for accountable leaders.

The arrangement has a long religious and institutional significance. Its later history includes disputes over representation and interpretation. Calling it a complete solution to every immediate and future problem would conceal the very work that later chapters need to explain.

9.4 — A hundred and two years

Set the two ends of this part beside each other.

In 1606 Guru Hargobind succeeded Guru Arjan after the latter's death under imperial authority. The tradition associates the sixth Guru with the two swords and the development of temporal responsibility alongside religious authority.

In 1708 the tenth Guru died at Nanded, after severe family losses in the preceding years. Sikh tradition recognises the Guru Granth Sahib and the Panth's collective responsibility after the line of ten human Gurus.

Between those dates the community experienced succession disputes, execution, armed conflict, institutional development and textual preservation. Each event requires its own sources. No claim about a universal monopoly on arms or the permanent removal of all hierarchy is necessary to see the period's importance.

Guru Gobind Singh was assassinated at Nanded and died on 7 October 1708, aged forty-one.

He ended the line of human Gurus and vested authority in the scripture — the Guru Granth Sahib — and in the community, the Guru Panth.

The transfer changed the form of Guruship and continuity. It did not make manuscripts impossible to alter, assemblies impossible to harm or institutional politics unnecessary. Reverence and a realistic account of later responsibilities fit together.

The tradition also associates Banda Singh Bahadur's commission with Nanded. His subsequent rise belongs to the next stage of political history rather than proof that every later dispute had already been solved.

The community endured persecution after 1708. Explaining that survival requires more than a claim that there was no head to remove. Congregations, leaders, texts, resources and local conditions all enter the history.

ph8-5-anandpur.html:
Anandpur

Anandpur placed a growing religious and political centre near the Shivalik foothills. Its location, local rulers, imperial power and the court's literary activity help explain the setting in which the tenth Guru's life and associated works are discussed.

5.1 — The position

Anandpur sits where the Shivalik foothills meet the Punjab plain, near the Sutlej.

That location is a compromise between two needs. Far enough into the hills to be defensible and outside easy Mughal administrative reach. Close enough to the plain that the community's people — who lived out there, in the villages and towns — could reach it.

Around it lay a scatter of small hill states, ruled by rajas who paid tribute to the empire when pressed and governed themselves the rest of the time.

The hill states are important to this history. Their rulers had territorial interests, revenue demands, rivalries and relationships with imperial power. They should not be reduced to a single motive or treated as interchangeable villains.

They ruled small territories with small revenues. They survived by not attracting imperial attention — paying what was demanded, keeping quiet, and settling their own disputes.

A growing armed community could affect a neighbouring ruler's authority, subjects and relations with the empire. Those practical interests are relevant alongside religious and personal considerations. Recognising them is a reason to study particular alignments, not to announce that belief never mattered.

From the rajas' side this is a serious problem whatever they think of the Guru's teaching. He is a rival power in territory they consider theirs, and his presence risks bringing a Mughal army into hills that had been left alone for generations.

The record contains changing conflicts and alliances. A small state might calculate its position between other powers. The calculation does not establish that conviction was absent; different motives can operate together.

5.2 — The fighting before 1699

Two engagements matter.

Bhangani, 1688. A coalition of hill rajas attacked the Guru's forces. He won. He was twenty-two, and it was his first battle.

Nadaun, 1691. Here the alignment reverses: the Guru fought alongside hill rajas against a Mughal commander sent to collect arrears of tribute. They won.

Changing alignments warn against a simple picture in which every participant's side is permanently determined by religious identity. The same ruler or group can occupy a different position at a later event.

The conventional accounts of Bhangani and Nadaun show differing alignments, and Muslim allies and soldiers also appear in accounts of the Guru's life. Each named participant and episode still needs its source; the larger lesson is that a collective religious label cannot explain every alliance.

Alliances formed and broke on immediate interest. The Guru fought Hindu rajas in 1688 and fought beside them against a Mughal force in 1691. His own army included Muslim soldiers — the sources name Pathan contingents in his service, and a Muslim commander who fought for him at Bhangani.

Politics involved territorial interests, power and particular circumstances as well as belief. A reader should resist both extremes: explaining every conflict as purely religious, or declaring that religion was irrelevant in every conflict.

5.3 — Poets and soldiers

The court at Anandpur was not only military.

The court is remembered as a centre of poets and scholars as well as soldiers. The number fifty-two belongs to later traditional descriptions; it is not used here as a securely reconstructed payroll. Works in several languages and forms require their own attribution and transmission histories.

A large literary corpus is associated with the tenth Guru and his milieu. Its devotional, martial and narrative forms should be distinguished. Part 6 examines why authorship, compilation and religious use do not always yield the same answer.

Dasam Granth: "the tenth book" — a large collection of compositions associated with Guru Gobind Singh, assembled after his death. It is distinct from the Guru Granth Sahib and does not have the same status.

The authorship of parts of it has been debated by scholars for over a century — some sections are broadly accepted as his, others are disputed as the work of court poets. This is a live scholarly question and it is worth knowing it exists.

5.4 — Why an army needs a reason

The purpose of all this was stated repeatedly in his own writing, and it is worth being precise about it because it is often flattened.

The Zafarnama's appeal to force is conditional and must be read within the letter. It should not be converted into permission for any act a later person calls a final resort. Identifying an ethical condition is only the beginning of assessing whether a particular action satisfies it.

The distinction between challenging unjust conduct and attacking a whole people is essential to the argument of this series. Individual passages and events should still be examined precisely, rather than using an attractive general description as a substitute for their evidence.

Anandpur sits where the Shivalik hills meet the plain — defensible, and still reachable by the community in the plains.

Changing hill-state alignments show why particular dates and actors matter. Practical interest can help explain an alliance without proving that no participant held convictions.

Accounts include Muslim helpers and fighters as well as Muslim opponents. They also include Hindu allies and opponents. A religious label alone is insufficient to reconstruct the sides at a particular encounter.

The court had substantial literary activity. Its remembered number of poets and the attribution of particular works require separate evidence. Honouring the literary setting does not require certainty about every later numerical description.

The doctrine of force in his own writing is conditional: legitimate only when every other means has failed — and directed against tyranny, not against a religion.

ph8-6-1699-the-khalsa.html:
1699: The Khalsa

The conventional account places the founding of the Khalsa at Vaisakhi 1699 at Anandpur. The event has a central religious significance. The exact theatrical and biographical details in later narration need to be distinguished from that broad historical account.

6.1 — What happened

In the received founding narrative, the Guru asks for a head and five volunteers respond. This is how the event is widely remembered. It is not a claim that every detail of the tent scene is independently documented by a surviving eyewitness record.

The familiar telling describes a bloodied sword and repeated requests before the five appear alive. Part 4 discusses why that narration is not enough to establish literal beheading and physical resurrection, or to prove what occurred out of view.

Then all five were brought out alive.

The five are remembered as the Panj Pyare — the five beloved.

Read that table twice, because both columns are the point.

The traditional geographical descriptions present the five as coming from widely separated places. Their significance in the received account is inclusion beyond one locality. That significance should not be converted into an exact map of congregational membership established by independent records for each participant.

The traditional descriptions also identify varied occupations and caste backgrounds. They communicate an important rejection of inherited rank within initiation. Those details should be labelled as the received account rather than treated as complete biographical archives.

The narrative emphasises that birth is not the qualification for commitment. It does not establish that every participant's social position has been independently documented, or that no person from such a background had ever borne arms before.

6.2 — The initiation

The Guru then initiated the five with a ceremony he devised.

Water was placed in an iron bowl and stirred with a khanda — a straight double-edged sword — while verses were recited. Sugar crystals were added, brought, according to tradition, by his wife. The five drank from the same bowl and were sprinkled with it.

Khande di pahul: the initiation ceremony — literally, the preparation by the double-edged sword. Often called amrit.

Khalsa: from a Persian and Arabic term meaning "pure", and also used administratively for land held directly by the crown rather than through an intermediary. Both senses are relevant: the initiated belong directly, with no one in between.

Singh and Kaur are important names in Sikh identity and discipline. Their use and the history of their wider adoption require attention to period. The current practice should not automatically be projected in every detail onto a single moment in 1699.

They were given a code of conduct and five items to keep on the body at all times: uncut hair, a comb, an iron bracelet, a particular undergarment, and a sword.

And then the Guru asked the five to initiate him.

He received the same ceremony from the men he had just created, and took the name Gobind Singh. The teacher took initiation from his own disciples.

6.3 — Why the names matter

Names can signal family, locality, caste and affiliation. A shared name can express a rejection of hierarchy. It does not automatically erase the other information people use to classify one another or the social practices through which discrimination continues.

Using Singh or Kaur can reduce the emphasis on caste in an introduction and express a shared commitment. It does not delete every caste association from family, marriage, property or institutional life.

A shared name can place a trader and a service-worker within the same religious identity. A stranger may still make assumptions from other information, and the people concerned may still face unequal treatment. Religious symbolism and a measured social outcome should be distinguished.

Singh had a history outside the Sikh community before its Sikh adoption. It was not a name whose every prior use can be reduced to an exclusive monopoly enforced identically over two thousand years.

The name's Sikh use can affirm dignity and a shared discipline. Its historical significance does not depend on the literal claim that nobody outside one caste had previously been permitted to use it.

6.4 — The right to carry a sword

Modern readers see the five items and read them as religious symbols — outward marks of belonging, comparable to a cross or a skullcap.

The assumption to question is that religious meaning and practical use must be alternatives. An article of discipline can have both, and its practical qualities do not erase its religious significance.

Look at the list again: a sword, an iron bracelet, an undergarment cut for movement, a comb, and long hair.

The articles include objects with practical uses, alongside their place in identity and discipline. They should not be reduced to a modern equipment list. The code gives them a religious context; invented physical mechanisms are neither necessary nor demonstrated by that context.

And the first item is the one that matters most, because of what it meant socially.

Texts describing hereditary social functions should not be treated as an exact census of who actually used weapons across South Asian history. People from varied backgrounds bore arms. The Khalsa's significance is an obligation within its discipline without a caste qualification, not the ending of a literally universal historical ban.

The Khalsa initiation required a sword of everyone who took it, regardless of birth — and gave them a warrior name to go with it.

A religious article can also carry a social challenge. The obligation to keep a kirpan affirms a particular discipline; its meaning should not be reduced either to empty decoration or to a claim that it alone immediately removed every hierarchy.

For someone denied dignity by inherited rank, recognition within a shared initiation can have substantial force. The ideal must still be assessed alongside later practice. It is an ethical demand to overcome discrimination, not proof that discrimination was completed and abolished everywhere in one day.

An armed tradition contributes to later mobilisation, but initiation does not establish that every member was equally equipped, trained or able to fight. Leaders, local networks and resources remained important to the community's survival.

6.5 — And the masands were abolished

One administrative change is easy to skip and should not be.

Guru Gobind Singh abolished the masand system — the network of regional representatives established by Guru Amar Das and developed under Guru Arjan, which The earlier Punjab history discusses.

The repudiation of the masands belongs to the institutional changes associated with the tenth Guru. Sikh sources describe abuses and rival loyalties. A uniform story in which every representative became corrupt in exactly the same way would overstate that evidence.

From then on, congregations dealt with the centre directly.

6.6 — What the Khalsa was for

It created a distinct religion

The Khalsa introduced a particularly visible and demanding form of discipline within a community that already had teaching, scripture, institutions and history. It did not create Sikh religious life from nothing, and not every Sikh became initiated.

It was a military reorganisation

Military mobilisation forms part of the context, but initiation also has religious meaning. The articles, names, vows and common ceremony cannot be explained completely by declaring theology unnecessary. An organisational interpretation and a religious interpretation can illuminate different aspects.

It completed what Nanak began

The common initiation expresses a rejection of inherited rank and the Guru's participation has a major place in its received meaning. The continued existence of caste practices means that expressing the principle was not the same as permanently removing hierarchy from the whole community.

The received founding narrative remembers the Panj Pyare as five volunteers from diverse backgrounds and places. It is a religiously important account whose exact details need their own source history.

Khande di pahul and the discipline of the articles have an important continuing place in Sikh life. Current practice is described in the code. Its details should not be used as automatic proof of every narrated detail in the founding scene.

Then the Guru asked them to initiate him.

The common identity challenges claims to dignity based only on inherited rank. Singh was not previously confined to an absolute monopoly across all periods, and adoption of the name did not make every later caste distinction disappear.

Changes in representation and initiation helped reshape the community. Its later resilience involved congregations, leaders, texts and resources. A requirement to keep the articles is not a universal historical register of military training.

ph8-8-the-zafarnama.html:
The Zafarnama

After severe losses, Guru Gobind Singh addressed Aurangzeb in a Persian letter known as the Zafarnama. Its argument about broken oaths and just conduct is worth reading without adding a claim that it caused every later event in the emperor's life.

8.1 — What it is

The letter is conventionally associated with the period following the evacuation of Anandpur and the ensuing losses. The dating, transmission and account of delivery should be examined through the relevant sources. Describing it as a preserved signed original would require evidence for that particular object.

It is written in Persian verse — the language of the empire, in the classical metre of Persian epic. It runs to just over a hundred couplets. It was carried south and, by the tradition, delivered.

It is called the Zafarnama — the letter of victory.

Start with the title, because the title is the argument.

The letter follows the loss of the Guru's four sons and mother, and the evacuation of his stronghold. These are severe losses. Saying that he literally had no followers, resources or agency left would be a rhetorical overstatement rather than an accurate account of what followed.

He calls the letter the letter of victory.

It addresses a powerful emperor in Persian, a language of imperial administration and literature. The choice allows the criticism to operate within a language the court understood. The argument does not require ranking Aurangzeb as the most powerful individual in the entire world.

8.2 — What it says

The letter makes four moves.

It accuses the emperor of oath-breaking. This is the central charge and it is pressed hard. Oaths were sworn on the Quran to secure the evacuation of Anandpur, and those oaths were broken. The letter tells Aurangzeb that a man who swears on his own scripture and then breaks the oath has dishonoured that scripture, not the person he deceived.

It challenges his religious standing. The argument turns Aurangzeb's own claim against him: a ruler who governs in the name of God and then acts without honour has forfeited the ground he stands on.

It states the conditions under which force is legitimate. This is the most quoted passage in the letter, and it says: when all other means of resolving a matter have been exhausted, it is lawful and right to take up the sword. The condition is as important as the permission.

The letter contests the meaning of victory by appealing to conduct and principle. Physical losses do not automatically settle the moral question. That is an interpretation of its argument, not proof that a political or military defeat had no real consequences.

Notice something unusual about the argument this letter makes, because it is easy to miss what is not in it.

It does not argue that the emperor's religion is false.

A conflict involving people of different religions need not be explained as a condemnation of an entire religion. The letter's criticism of broken oaths is directed at conduct. The critic should read that argument rather than attach a whole-community accusation to it.

The Zafarnama does the opposite. It holds him to his own scripture. The charge is not that the Quran is wrong; it is that the emperor swore on it and then lied, and that this is an offence against the book he swore on.

The assumption the letter refuses is that a conflict between people of two religions must be a conflict between the religions.

The accounts of Muslim allies and helpers discussed in Part 4 also resist a whole-community explanation of the conflict. Each story and its details still require their own evidence. A broad ethical interpretation cannot do that verification automatically.

The distinction between judging conduct and condemning an entire people remains useful for reading later history. It is a principle for the reader's own reasoning, not an assurance that every later actor consistently observed it.

8.3 — Is it genuine?

The letter is included in the collection of compositions associated with Guru Gobind Singh, and its authenticity is broadly accepted, though — like other parts of that collection — it has been examined by scholars.

The letter's content, transmission and relationship to early accounts are relevant to assessing attribution. Literary quality alone is not proof of a particular author. Nor is an assertion that no later devotee could have written a difficult admission; claims about what unknown writers could never invent are not reliable evidence.

8.4 — What happened next

Aurangzeb died in March 1707, aged eighty-eight, after twenty-six years of ruinous war in the Deccan. The succession was disputed among his sons.

Guru Gobind Singh met the eventual winner, Bahadur Shah, and relations were cordial. He travelled south with the imperial camp into the Deccan.

The Persian letter follows severe personal and political losses and contests the moral meaning of victory. Those circumstances give it force without the exaggeration that its author had literally nothing left.

It accuses him of breaking oaths sworn on the Quran, and argues that the dishonour falls on the man who swore, not on the man deceived.

Its most quoted lines state that force is legitimate only when every other means has failed — the condition being as important as the permission.

It does not attack Islam. It holds the emperor to his own scripture. The line drawn is between just and unjust conduct, not between religions.

Aurangzeb died in March 1707.

ph7-3-kartarpur-turning-teaching-into-an.html:
Kartarpur: Turning Teaching Into an Institution

At Kartarpur the teaching was expressed through a settled community and shared practices. These institutions matter alongside the compositions. Their history shows how a tradition is lived and transmitted, without the absolute claim that ideas always die unless one particular institutional form is built.

3.1 — Settling down

Around 1520 Nanak settled at a place on the Ravi that came to be called Kartarpur — "the creator's town".

He farmed. He led daily gatherings, morning and evening, with singing of his compositions. And around him a settled community formed of people who had come to live near him.

Three institutions took shape there.

3.2 — Sangat, pangat, langar

Sangat: the congregation. The gathered community of followers. In this tradition, spiritual life is something you do together, not alone.

Langar: the free kitchen. Food cooked and served to everyone who comes, without charge and without conditions.

Pangat: the row. Everyone sits on the floor in a line to eat — the same food, at the same level, in the same room.

Open kitchens were not unique to Sikh life. Langar's place alongside congregation and shared seating has a specific Sikh history and meaning. That meaning does not require proving that no shared row of diners had existed anywhere previously.

Pangat, shared seating, gives the principle a visible practice. The significance lies in refusing unequal access and treatment at the meal. It should be described without a claim to have demonstrated the first such arrangement in all human history.

To see why sitting in a row matters, you have to understand what eating meant in this society.

Rules about commensality and touch have been important instruments of caste hierarchy. Their operation varies with setting and period. A shared meal can challenge those rules at the place where they affect everyday conduct.

The act can make a teaching concrete. It does not by itself remove every social hierarchy outside the meal. That is why examining who cooks, who serves and who exercises authority remains important.

A shared practice can let participants experience a principle together. Different communities have different food rules and histories; participation should not be described as an identical break with an identical social order for every person.

That is why langar is the institution rather than the charity. The feeding is real and matters. The seating arrangement is the teaching.

The earlier Punjab history explains Guru Amar Das making this explicit by requiring that anyone who wished to meet him must first eat in the langar — including, according to tradition, a Mughal emperor.

3.3 — The succession

Guru Nanak's choice of Angad rather than one of his sons is central to Sikh succession. The detailed tests narrated in the janamsakhis should be distinguished from the succession itself. A later moral account of a test is not automatically an independently confirmed scene.

Nanak had two sons. The elder, Sri Chand, was an ascetic of genuine reputation who later founded his own order. The younger was Lakhmi Das.

He passed over both.

He chose a follower named Lehna, who had come to him some years earlier, and who had shown — in the janamsakhi accounts — an absolute readiness to do whatever was asked, however menial or strange, without calculation.

Nanak renamed him Angad, from a word meaning "limb" or "part of my own body", installed him publicly, bowed to him, and made the transfer unmistakable.

This is one of the most consequential decisions in the history of Punjab, and it is easy to walk past.

Many offices and assets passed through family relationships, but discipleship succession also existed in the wider religious landscape. Nanak's choice is important within this tradition without the universal claim that every other position in fifteenth-century society had to pass to a son.

It said: this is not property, and it is not a family's possession. It goes to whoever is fit for it.

The succession helped the teaching continue in an identifiable community. That result does not prove that every teaching inherited by a son usually fails, or that every chosen disciple succeeds. Historical explanation should avoid turning one significant choice into an unsupported law of all institutions.

Sri Chand and the Udasi tradition belong to the wider history of relationships with the Sikh community. Their later institutional life should not be reduced to a single permanent family grievance or a claim that every Udasi practice has one motive.

Religious history is usually told as the story of founders. The founder has the vision; everything after is described as spreading it, or as decline from it.

The assumption is that the ideas are the important part, and the institutions are just plumbing.

Comparable arguments in bhagat compositions form part of the devotional landscape. Similarity does not make their traditions identical, and no global population comparison is needed to justify studying Sikh institutional development.

Institutional development helps explain continuity, alongside the teaching and the people who received it. A population total is not a measure of the quality of an idea, and other devotional communities should not be dismissed because this chapter does not survey their scale.

Succession, congregation, langar, towns, scripts, compilation and resources all contributed to Sikh continuity. This is a plural explanation. It should not be turned into a claim that the teaching's merit played no part, or that infrastructure alone explains every outcome.

The relationship between teaching and organisation is the point. Practices give people ways to receive and act on an idea. Institutions can preserve it, and they can also fail it; their existence is not proof that every stated principle is already realised.

3.4 — And then he died

Nanak died at Kartarpur in 1539.

Guru Nanak died at Kartarpur in 1539 in the conventional chronology. The story of a dispute over the funeral is part of devotional memory. Its meaning can be discussed without asserting that its literal details have been established independently.

Nanak settled at Kartarpur around 1520 and farmed for the last two decades of his life, leading a community.

Three institutions: sangat (the congregation), langar (the free kitchen), pangat (everyone eating in a row).

Langar existed in Sufi lodges already. Pangat is the radical part — because caste ran on rules about who may cook for, touch and sit beside whom, and a shared row breaks it exactly where it operates.

Passing Guruship to Angad was consequential for continuity. The detailed narrated tests and gestures should be identified by their source tradition rather than all given an identical level of verification.

Institutional work and teaching belong together. The succession is part of why a continuing Sikh tradition developed; it is not an exclusive explanation that removes every other cause.

ph7-4-three-gurus-who-built-the-structur.html:
Three Gurus Who Built the Structure

The work of Guru Angad, Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das shows successive institutional development. Their contributions deserve attention alongside the more frequently retold spectacular episodes. Describing this as the most important period is an interpretation, not a ranking that the sources require every reader to accept.

4.1 — Guru Angad (1539–1552)

Angad moved the centre to Khadur and did three things.

The early preservation and collection of compositions form part of the history leading to the Adi Granth. The exact relationships among surviving collections and manuscripts need their own examination. It would be too simple to say that every later line rests on one perfectly documented collection made at one moment.

He standardised the Gurmukhi script. Chapter 5 is entirely about why this matters.

Traditional accounts associate Guru Angad with educational and physical activities. Those accounts can illuminate the community's ideals. They should be distinguished from an exact surviving register of schools, pupils and exercise grounds.

4.2 — Guru Amar Das (1552–1574)

He became Guru at seventy-three and held it for twenty-two years, and he was the organiser.

He moved the centre to Goindwal on the Beas and had a baoli dug there — a large step-well with a long flight of steps down to the water.

Baoli: a step-well. A well with a staircase running down to the water, so people can walk to it as the level drops through the year. A major piece of public infrastructure in dry regions, and expensive to build.

Then he did something with much longer consequences: he divided the community's territory into administrative districts, each under an appointed representative.

Manji: literally a small cot or seat. Used for the twenty-two districts Guru Amar Das established, each with a representative who taught, led the local congregation, and connected it to the centre.

The manji system is remembered as a network of teaching and representation under Guru Amar Das. Manji literally means a small cot or seat. The later masand system developed further mechanisms of representation and contributions; the terms should not be treated as identical at every date.

This is the moment a scattered following becomes a structure.

A network can connect dispersed followers to a centre through teaching, communication and resources. That is an institutional development, not evidence that the centre held a precise membership record for every village.

After it: a network. Each district has someone responsible. Instructions go out; contributions come in. Somebody in a distant village belongs to something with a shape, and the centre knows they exist.

Representation can create practical questions about accountability and resources. The later rejection of masands should be studied through Sikh sources, not explained by a universal assertion that every distant collector inevitably becomes corrupt.

Representatives may acquire competing interests over time. Whether that happened in a particular place and period requires evidence. The tenth Guru's repudiation of masands is not proof of an identical career and motive for every earlier representative.

Amar Das also made three decisions that pushed the community further towards being distinct.

He made langar compulsory before an audience. Anyone who wished to see the Guru had to eat in the kitchen first, sitting in the row. There was no exemption for rank. This converts Chapter 3's principle into an enforced rule at the door.

He acted against sati and purdah and encouraged the remarriage of widows — carrying Nanak's argument about women into social practice.

He established distinct gathering days, calling the community together at particular times of year. Small in itself, large in effect: a community that assembles on its own calendar is on its way to being a separate one.

4.3 — Guru Ram Das (1574–1581)

Guru Ram Das held office for only seven years and founded a city.

He established a settlement that came to be called Ramdaspur and later Amritsar, and began excavating the great pool at its centre. The earlier Punjab history explains what he started.

Guru Ram Das composed the Lavan received in the Guru Granth Sahib. Their later central place in Anand Karaj is important. Composition date and the full later ceremonial arrangement are distinct questions; the existence of hymns alone does not establish every detail of an unchanged rite from their first composition.

4.4 — The succession changes shape

From Guru Ram Das onwards, Guruship passed within the Sodhi family, with particular succession disputes and changes of branch. Guru Har Krishan's succession by Guru Tegh Bahadur, for example, was not a simple automatic father-to-son inheritance. Family connection and recognition as Guru require distinct descriptions.

A retreat from the original principle

One interpretation emphasises the tension between an initial discipleship succession and later family relationships. That tension deserves discussion, but calling Guruship merely family property would assume the very conclusion being debated.

A solution to a real problem

Another interpretation emphasises the sitting Guru's choice and the community's recognition, rather than automatic primogeniture. Both religious meaning and family relationships matter. A narrator should not infer every appointment's private motive from the relationship alone.

Angad collected Nanak's hymns, standardised Gurmukhi, and set up schools and exercise grounds.

Amar Das was the organiser: the baoli at Goindwal, twenty-two districts with appointed representatives, langar made compulsory before an audience, action against sati and purdah, and separate gathering days.

Ram Das founded Amritsar and composed the marriage hymns still used today.

Family connections and rival claims are part of the succession history. They are not sufficient to reduce the compilation of scripture to one family dispute. The religious and preservation purposes also need their place in the explanation.

ph7-6-amritsar-a-city-built-around-a-poo.html:
Amritsar: A City Built Around a Pool

The settlement and sarovar associated with Guru Ram Das developed into a major religious and commercial centre. Guru Arjan's work at Harmandir Sahib gave the setting further institutional significance. The building's received symbolism should be distinguished from claims to know the exact intention behind every design decision.

6.1 — The founding

Around 1577, Guru Ram Das established a settlement on land in central Punjab and began excavating a large pool — a sarovar.

The town was first called Ramdaspur. It took its later name from the pool: Amritsar, the pool of nectar.

A grant from Akbar

One tradition describes an imperial grant; another describes purchase from local proprietors. The sources and their dates need examination. A political interpretation that prefers one account is not independent evidence that the account must be correct.

Purchased from local villagers

The purchase account connects the settlement to contributions and local transactions. Its plausibility is not proof. The reader should be able to distinguish a coherent explanation from a surviving document establishing the exact transaction.

6.2 — Why a pool

A sarovar in this period was a familiar thing — sacred tanks were built at religious sites across India. But this one was placed at the centre of the settlement and made the reason for the town's existence, rather than an addition to a temple.

Stored water has practical uses in settlement life as well as a religious significance at this site. That observation does not establish that this sarovar was primarily designed as the town's municipal drinking-water supply; a specific engineering history would require more evidence.

6.3 — Guru Arjan's decisions

Under Guru Arjan, from 1581, the pool was lined and a shrine was built in the middle of it, reached by a causeway. This is the building later known as the Harmandir Sahib.

Three features of it are arguments in architecture.

It has a door on each of the four sides. The standard reading is that it is open in every direction, to people of every kind — and specifically not oriented so as to admit some and exclude others.

Visitors descend toward the shrine. A received interpretation connects this with humility. Comparing the design with every religious building in India would require a much wider architectural survey than this chapter has performed.

It sits in water. Approached along a causeway with the pool on both sides.

Architecture can communicate meanings to worshippers. It can also acquire interpretations across time. Explaining a meaningful interpretation is not the same as proving an original design brief or declaring every other building's symbolism identical.

Four doors: there is no back entrance and no side for particular castes. Every approach is the main approach.

The descent is commonly understood through humility. Other Indian religious structures have varied arrangements, including structures approached downwards. The argument does not require the false universal statement that the sacred is always approached by climbing.

A shared route and shared space can express equal access. The symbolism becomes more effective when the actual treatment of visitors matches it. A building's arrangement is not by itself a measurement that every social barrier has disappeared.

A widely held tradition holds that the foundation was laid by Mian Mir, a Sufi of Lahore. Some historians accept it; others note that it appears in relatively late sources and treat it cautiously. What is not in dispute is that the tradition exists and has been meaningful for centuries — and that relations between the Gurus and Sufi figures of Lahore were real, which is why the story was plausible enough to take root.

6.4 — And it was a city, not only a shrine

This part is often skipped and it matters.

Guru Arjan deliberately built Amritsar as a working town. He encouraged traders and craftsmen to settle, developed markets, and made it a place of commerce as well as devotion. Bazaars grew around the pool. It became a centre for horse trading, among other things.

Dasvandh is commonly understood as contributing a tenth of earnings for religious and community purposes. Its practice and channels require their own historical and contemporary descriptions. It should not be presented as a purchase that guarantees spiritual favour.

Dasvandh: "a tenth". The practice of giving a tenth of one's earnings to the community's common fund. Formalised under Guru Arjan.

Systematic contributions can support shared institutions. The precise scale and flow at a given date should not be asserted without records. The existence of a contribution practice is not an exact annual budget for the whole early community.

Resources help institutions survive and develop. A funded project can still need accountable management. The relation between contributions and particular buildings, compilations or services requires evidence where an exact financial claim is made.

Community support can reduce dependence on a single patron. It does not guarantee complete independence from every ruler, and a grant does not automatically prove that a recipient has surrendered its teaching. Political relationships need examination rather than a universal rule about funding.

And it made the community visible in a way it had not been. By 1600 there was a town, a treasury, a network of officials, a distinct script, its own marriage rite, and a scripture in preparation.

By the early seventeenth century, settlement, sacred space, collections of teaching and networks of contribution gave the community an identifiable institutional life. The encounter with imperial power should be read through its own sources, rather than an imagined moment when the government first noticed.

Guru Ram Das founded Amritsar around 1577 and began digging the pool. Whether the land was granted by Akbar or bought by the community is genuinely disputed.

Under Guru Arjan the shrine was built in the middle of the pool — four doors, and set below the surrounding ground so you walk down to it rather than up.

The shrine's four-sided access and descent are meaningful in Sikh interpretation. They can be explained without declaring that almost every other Indian religious building has exactly the opposite arrangement.

Amritsar developed as a working town around a sacred centre. Contributions supported community life, alongside the other economic and political relationships of the period. No single architectural feature automatically proves all those relationships.

The institutions made the community visible and durable. Later conflict cannot be reduced to an unsupported claim that visibility alone caused it; imperial decisions, local relationships and particular events require their own evidence.

ph7-2-what-nanak-taught.html:
What Nanak Taught

This reading begins with received compositions attributed to Guru Nanak, not a summary of every later Sikh practice. It explains selected arguments in ordinary language. English renderings here are explanatory paraphrases, and the linked original locations should be consulted for the wording and context.

2.1 — Where he starts

The opening of the Guru Granth Sahib is a short statement that functions as the foundation of everything after it. It begins with Ik Onkar — one being, one reality.

What follows sets out that this reality is true, is the creator, is without fear and without hatred, is beyond time and beyond birth and death, is self-existent, and is realised through the grace of the guru.

Ik Onkar opens the scripture and is a central expression of the divine unity in Sikh interpretation. A short English rendering cannot exhaust its meaning. The numeral one and the expression following it should be read in the religious context of the opening rather than as a modern scientific formula.

Nam: literally "name", but in this usage closer to the divine reality itself as it can be held in human awareness. Nam simran — remembrance of the name — is the central practice.

Hukam: the divine order or command. The way things are. Living in harmony with it, rather than fighting it out of ego, is a constant theme.

Haumai: "I-am-ness". Ego, self-centredness. In Nanak's verses this is the fundamental human problem — the wall between a person and reality.

2.2 — Against ritual as a substitute

This is the theme that appears most often and most sharply.

His argument is not that religious practice is worthless. It is that the outward act cannot do the inward work, and that people constantly use the first to avoid the second.

He goes after bathing at holy places, pilgrimage, fasting, sacred marks and threads, ritual purity, and formal prayer performed without attention — and he goes after them in both traditions. The pandit and the mullah are criticised in the same terms, and often in the same verse.

The recurring move is to take a ritual object and redefine it as an inner quality. If you must wear a sacred thread, he says in effect, let it be spun from compassion and twisted with contentment — a thread like that does not break, burn or wear out. If you must be a true Muslim, then let mercy be your mosque and honest labour your prayer.

The argument can be expressed through an everyday example. That example illustrates a distinction between outward performance and conduct; it is not a historical explanation that proves why the teaching spread.

A man bathes in a holy river every morning and cheats his neighbour every afternoon. Another performs every prayer at the right hour and treats his servants as less than human.

Nanak's question is simply: what has the ritual actually done?

Criticism of empty outward performance can challenge institutions and habits, including those inside a religious community. It should not be used to assert that every religious specialist lives dishonestly or that every establishment has always responded with hostility.

2.3 — Against caste

Nanak's rejection of caste is direct and it is not incidental.

His position, argued repeatedly: caste has no standing before God; it will count for nothing at the reckoning; pride in high birth is simply another form of ego; and it is conduct, not birth, that makes a person high or low. In one much-quoted passage he identifies himself with the lowest of the low rather than with the high.

Shared practices, including congregation and langar, give the principle an institutional expression. The continuing presence of caste distinctions means that creating a practice was not the same as finishing the whole social task.

2.4 — On women

One passage is quoted more than any other, and it is worth being precise about what it says.

The argument runs: it is from woman that we are conceived and born; to woman we are engaged and married; woman is our friend and from woman comes the family; when one woman dies another is sought; we are bound to the world through woman. So why call her inferior, when she gives birth to kings?

The passage challenges contempt through the ordinary dependence of life on women. Later Sikh tradition also remembers reforms associated with Guru Amar Das. Neither a scriptural argument nor a remembered reform establishes that every later community has already achieved equal treatment.

2.5 — Stay in the world

The compositions engage ascetic practices and the relation between spiritual life and household life. A comparison should identify the particular position being addressed rather than making every yogi or Nath follow one uniform doctrine.

Renunciation and bodily disciplines were important in several ascetic traditions, with substantial internal variety. The dialogue in the Sikh compositions should be read as an encounter with particular claims and practices, not a census of every ascetic's belief.

Nanak's answer was that it is possible, and better, to live in the middle of ordinary life and remain unattached: to work, marry, raise children, deal honestly, and hold the divine in mind throughout. The image he uses is the lotus, which grows in muddy water and is not stained by it.

Later tradition summarised the practical form of this in three phrases: work honestly, remember the divine, share what you have. The wording is later. The substance is all through the verses, and Kartarpur is what it looked like in practice.

2.6 — On rulers

He was not politically quiet, and one group of hymns proves it.

When Babur invaded in the early 1520s, Nanak appears to have witnessed the destruction of a town in Punjab. Four hymns describe it: the killing, the women of the town whose lives were destroyed, the collapse of an order that had believed itself secure.

What is remarkable is that the criticism runs in every direction at once. Babur's soldiers are described committing atrocities. But the Lodhi rulers are also condemned — for their luxury, their negligence, their failure to defend the people who depended on them. And the hymns put the question to God directly, asking how such suffering was permitted.

These hymns are unusual evidence and worth flagging as such.

The Babarvani compositions are received as Guru Nanak's response to the suffering associated with invasion. They provide a religious and poetic voice addressing violence. Reconstructing the exact place and circumstances of every passage requires attention to the biographical and historical sources.

These compositions give attention to suffering beyond royal achievement. That is valuable without the comparative claim that almost every other surviving work of the period was only a court chronicle.

A lament can preserve concern for captives, women and ordinary people. It is not a complete administrative record. Poetry and contemporary records can contribute different evidence to an account of the period.

The limitation: they are poetry, composed to be sung, using the language of lament. They are not a report, and specific details cannot be pressed hard.

2.7 — Was he founding a religion?

He was founding something new

The succession, compositions and community associated with Guru Nanak are important evidence for the development of a distinct tradition. Claims about precisely how he privately conceived every future boundary are harder to establish. The historical development should not be forced into a modern administrative category projected unchanged backwards.

The category did not exist as we mean it

The terms used to describe religion and community have histories. People in the period had real distinctions as well as overlapping practices. Modern classification can illuminate some questions and distort others; it would be wrong to say that nobody had religious identities or boundaries before modernity.

It begins with Ik Onkar — one reality. The central practice is remembrance; the central problem is ego.

Against ritual as a substitute for inner change — attacking pandit and mullah in the same breath, and redefining ritual objects as inner qualities.

Against caste, plainly, and followed up with an institution rather than left as a statement.

Stay in the world. Work, marry, deal honestly, remember. Not withdrawal — which is where he parts from the yogis.

The invasion compositions criticise suffering and failures of rule. They should be read as poetry with historical significance, not as an exact report that independently establishes every detail of the familiar life narrative.

ph10-6-what-his-punjab-was-actually-like.html:
What His Punjab Was Actually Like

To live in it, rather than to read about it. This chapter is about who the population actually were, what the state took from them, and whether "golden age" survives contact with the evidence.

6.1 — Who lived there

Start with the fact that most accounts skip, because it changes the meaning of everything else.

The kingdom ruled by Ranjit Singh contained a Muslim majority, substantial Hindu populations and a Sikh minority. Exact proportions depend on boundaries and available evidence; no precise religious census of an unchanged territory is supplied here.

So this was a state in which a religious minority held political and military power over a large majority, across a territory stretching from the Khyber to the Sutlej and including Kashmir, Multan and the Derajat, whose populations were overwhelmingly Muslim.

Hold that fact next to Chapter 3's court.

A Muslim foreign minister and Hindu finance minister are important evidence of the court's diversity. They do not prove that this was the only conceivable form of government or that every subject experienced inclusion equally.

It also reframes what a "Sikh empire" means. It was a state ruled by Sikhs. It was not a Sikh country, in the sense of most of its people being Sikhs — and the phrase misleads badly if you carry the modern idea of a nation into it.

The distinction between the ruler's religion and the population's composition matters for the whole period. A label such as Sikh empire should not make the reader imagine a territory in which nearly everyone followed the ruler's religion.

6.2 — What the state took

Revenue was the business of government, and the demand was heavy.

The state took a large share of the crop — the proportion varied by region and by year, and in the richest districts it was very substantial. Collection was frequently farmed out: the right to collect a district's revenue was auctioned to a contractor, who paid the state a fixed sum and kept whatever more he could extract.

Revenue farming means assigning the right to collect revenue under an agreement, often for a payment to the state. The arrangement can shift collection work and create incentives for extraction. It does not literally eliminate all administrative cost or oversight in every case.

A collector seeking a surplus can have an incentive to impose heavier demands. The arrangement and its consequences vary with contract, tenure and enforcement. Describing that incentive is more precise than assuming that every collector had no interest in a district's future.

Such arrangements occurred in many states. Their results require evidence about particular regions and periods. They should not be described as inevitably producing the maximum conceivable misery everywhere.

6.3 — Justice

Most disputes were settled where they had always been settled — by village councils, caste bodies and local custom. Serious matters went to the district official, and above him to the governor and ultimately the court at Lahore.

Several observers emphasise Ranjit Singh's reluctance to order executions. That reputation deserves attention, but a claim that every European visitor reported it identically would require inspecting all their accounts.

The ruler is often described as avoiding capital punishment in his personal judicial practice. That does not establish that nobody died at the hands of the state, its armies or its governors. Punishment, warfare and the conduct of provincial officials are separate questions.

Accounts describing restraint in executions can contribute to an assessment of the ruler. They do not cancel other kinds of coercion or demonstrate that every observer agreed about every part of the reign.

6.4 — Kashmir

The conquered provinces are where the honest account has to be least comfortable, and Kashmir is the hardest case.

Kashmir under Sikh rule was governed as a conquered territory and taxed heavily. Its main industry — the fine shawl weaving for which it was famous across the world — was taxed at a level that damaged it, and weavers emigrated in numbers.

Kashmir experienced severe famine and distress during the period, with conditions differing from the court's perspective. Exact dating and scale require the relevant regional accounts. A broad claim that all contemporary testimony is uniformly negative would overstate the material examined.

Peshawar was held under a governor whose methods were notorious even by the standards of the time.

Yes, by the standards of what came before and around it

A case for the reign's achievements can point to a durable state, commerce, patronage and officials of varied religions. It should not claim forty years without internal conflict, permanent closure of every invasion route, or total absence of abuses throughout every province.

It was a well-run conquest state, which is different

A critical account should include revenue demands, the conditions of conquered territories and coercive government. It need not deny every achievement at the capital. The right question is how different people and places experienced the same state.

The Sikh ruler governed a religiously diverse population with a Muslim majority. That distinction should remain visible when the kingdom is described by the ruler's religious affiliation.

Revenue demand was heavy, and collection was often farmed out to contractors who profited from squeezing.

Ranjit Singh's reputation for restraint in ordering executions does not make the entire state free of lethal violence or harsh punishment. Examine particular actions and officials alongside the reputation.

Conditions in Kashmir and Peshawar complicate a uniformly celebratory account. Taxation, famine and coercion require regional attention rather than a statement that every subject shared the court's prosperity.

Ask how the reign looked from different positions. A merchant, court official, cultivator or shawl worker could experience it differently. A fair assessment can recognise achievements and serious costs without forcing a single experience on everyone.

ph7-10-an-honest-list-of-what-we-do-not-.html:
Where a careful account leaves questions open

The early community has substantial scriptural evidence alongside biographies and accounts of institutions. The strengths differ by question. A received composition is a different kind of evidence from a later narrated scene. Neither should be forced to answer every historical question.

Guru Nanak's broad chronology and succession can be described, while a precise route and date for every journey remain harder to establish. The janamsakhi traditions differ, and a complete travel schedule should not be inferred from joining their longest versions together. A named place associated with a remembered visit is not by itself an independently dated itinerary.
