The founding and development of Amritsar are significant. The exact land transaction and the later foundation story have disputed details and source histories. A preference for community purchase or imperial grant cannot replace the relevant documentary evidence. The original Part 3's categorical wording about Mian Mir is qualified in Part 13.

Guru Arjan's death under imperial authority is distinct from a reconstruction of every act, word and expression in custody. Accounts from different settings must be read together and their limitations named. A contemporary imperial perspective is not neutral merely because it is contemporary; a later Sikh account is not automatically useless merely because it is later.

Numbers of followers and exact levels of literacy are difficult to reconstruct without membership and educational records. The existence of congregations, scriptural transmission and representatives establishes institutional activity. It does not establish a modern census of every person who identified with the community.

The compositions make a religious voice available in quantity. That voice can address ordinary conduct, labour and suffering. It is still poetry and teaching, not a complete register of every social interaction. A concern for dignity in the text should lead the reader to investigate conduct rather than assume all conduct already matched it.

Standardisation of a script and compilation of a corpus helped transmission. They did not remove the need to learn vocabulary and grammar, investigate manuscripts or explain interpretive disagreement. Direct access becomes more useful through good teaching. Telling a beginner that knowing the letters makes every passage self-evident can leave the beginner less able to recognise a misleading explanation.

Questions left open should be precise. Not securely verified in the record examined is a limited conclusion. It should not become never happened, everybody invented it, or no historical information exists anywhere. Equally, an absence of a refutation does not establish a narrated miracle as proved fact.

That discipline applies to favourable and unfavourable statements alike. An admiring writer can exaggerate literacy, equality or the firstness of a reform. A hostile writer can exaggerate ignorance, cruelty or uniformity. Both writers owe the reader the source and the limits. The shared task is an account that survives a reader opening the evidence.

ph9-1-banda-singh-bahadur.html:
Banda Singh Bahadur

Banda Singh Bahadur's mobilisation after the tenth Guru's death led to a short-lived challenge to Mughal authority and the capture of Sirhind in 1710. Accounts also associate his rule with changes benefiting cultivators. Their precise extent should not be inflated into the claim that no earlier Indian ruler had ever altered landholding.

1.1 — Who he was

He was born around 1670 in the hill country of Rajouri, in what is now Jammu, and named Lachhman Dev. He left home young, became an ascetic, and eventually settled at Nanded on the Godavari, far south in the Deccan, where he lived as a holy man under the name Madho Das.

In September 1708, Guru Gobind Singh — who was at Nanded with the imperial camp — went to see him.

The conventional Sikh account associates his commission with the tenth Guru at Nanded. Narrated details of their meeting belong to their source traditions. His subsequent mobilisation and campaigns provide a separate historical record that does not depend on confirming every scene of that meeting.

Weeks later the Guru was dead. Banda went to Punjab anyway.

Hukamnama: a written order or letter of command issued under a Guru's authority. Banda carried these, addressed to Sikh congregations in Punjab, instructing them to support him.

A recognised commission could help a newcomer mobilise existing congregations. That is an institutional explanation, not proof that one letter alone supplied every resource and relationship needed to raise a force.

1.2 — Two years

His mobilisation involved groups with varied interests and grievances. It should not be described as though every recruit had the same experience, motive or literally nothing to lose.

The campaign moved fast. Sonipat. Samana, in November 1709 — the town from which the executioners of Guru Tegh Bahadur and the Guru's younger sons had come, and which was sacked. Then a string of towns across the eastern Punjab plain.

In May 1710 he met the main Mughal force at Chappar Chiri, outside Sirhind.

Wazir Khan died in the fighting and Sirhind fell. The scale and extent of destruction need their own evidence; the survival of structures and the chronology of rebuilding complicate the phrase that the whole city was simply destroyed. The deaths of the younger Sahibzadas are conventionally dated in Sikh institutional accounts to December 1705, while other chronologies differ.

Measure the speed of this.

The losses following Anandpur were severe, and imperial persecution forms part of the period's history. They do not establish that the Guru or the whole community literally possessed no resources, followers or organisation afterwards.

Within a short period of mobilisation, Banda's forces captured Sirhind. The achievement deserves attention without a precise nineteen-month calculation dependent on a disputed starting date.

Discontent, existing Sikh networks, military choices and the changing reach of imperial power all help explain the mobilisation. An explanation should leave room for these factors rather than presenting anger alone as a complete cause.

1.3 — What he did with it

This is the part that matters, and it is usually reduced to a single line about revenge.

He established a government. He took a hill fort north of Sirhind, renamed it Lohgarh, and made it his capital. He appointed administrators. He issued orders under his own seal.

He struck coins. And the inscription on them is remarkable: it puts the victory in the names of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh — not in Banda's own name.

Accounts describe displacement of some established intermediaries and benefits to cultivators. The extent, duration and local operation of these measures require careful evidence. The brief and contested territory should not be presented as a uniformly documented abolition of every landholding arrangement.

Zamindar: literally "landholder". Under the Mughal system, an intermediary who held rights over land and collected revenue from the cultivators, keeping a share and passing the rest up. The position was hereditary and gave enormous local power.

Intermediaries could exercise substantial power over cultivators. Their rights and the cultivators' options varied. Saying there was no appeal anywhere would oversimplify a complex revenue and judicial system.

The historical association of Banda with cultivator interests is significant. The available account does not establish that every cultivator in every controlled area received an identical, securely recorded ownership grant.

Changes in access to land can transform lives. To assess this particular case, the reader needs to distinguish an important remembered political measure from a comprehensive surviving register of beneficiaries.

Describing the measures as benefiting cultivators is more defensible than a universal claim that landlordism was abolished across all the territory in a single fully documented settlement.

Comparisons with later land reform require consistent definitions, territories and outcomes. This chapter does not establish that no reform occurred anywhere in India between 1710 and the 1950s, or that every later effort simply failed.

Consider what it does. A farmer who owns his land keeps what he grows above the tax. He has a reason to improve it. He has a reason to defend it. And he has a reason to support whoever gave it to him.

A challenge to established revenue interests can provoke resistance, alongside a challenge to political authority. It is an explanatory possibility supported by the nature of the conflict, not proof of the exclusive motive of every imperial actor.

The connection between social dignity and political measures is worth examining. It does not require the false claim that arms had been universally unavailable to all but one hereditary group before the Khalsa.

1.4 — The war, and the end

The empire responded in force. Bahadur Shah brought an army north in 1710–11 and issued orders for Sikhs to be killed wherever found. Banda lost Lohgarh, retreated into the hills, came back, took territory again, and was pushed back again.

The war ran for six years across eastern Punjab and the Shivaliks.

In 1715 he was besieged at Gurdas Nangal, near Gurdaspur. The siege lasted around eight months. The defenders ran out of food entirely; the accounts describe them eating leaves, bark and finally their animals.

He was captured in December 1715 with several hundred followers, paraded to Delhi, and executed there in June 1716. The manner of it was deliberately public and deliberately prolonged. His young son was killed in front of him.

The record includes imperial reporting, historical narratives and material evidence. Their relationship and independence must be examined. A list of three categories should not automatically be counted as three independent confirmations of every detail.

Imperial newsletters can contribute dates and official responses where relevant records survive. They remain institutional sources with perspectives and omissions. Their administrative tone is useful but does not make them neutral or incapable of error.

Persian narratives can contribute evidence, including accounts written from an unfriendly standpoint. Hostility does not make a statement automatically true. The passage should be assessed for proximity, purpose, transmission and agreement with other evidence.

Coins and seals associated with this political tradition can establish particular claims of authority. A material object still needs provenance, dating and a careful reading of its inscription; it is not interpretation-free merely because it is physical.

Where the evidence is thin: his own thinking. We have what he did and what he minted. We have almost nothing about why, in his own voice.

1.5 — The argument about him

Banda's standing has been debated within the tradition since his own lifetime, and the dispute is old rather than modern.

He deviated

Contemporary criticism from some Sikhs held that he had set himself up as a leader in a way that came close to claiming the authority the tenth Guru had just placed in the scripture and the community. Some accounts describe followers of his adopting distinct practices and a distinct greeting, and a split opening between his followers and others.

Guru Gobind Singh had ended the line of Gurus deliberately. A charismatic commander governing in his own right, however loyal, sits awkwardly with that.

He did what he was sent to do

The commission, campaigns and remembered endurance contribute to the importance of Banda in Sikh history. They do not make every disputed practice or relationship automatically settled in his favour. A reader can recognise the historical role while examining the actual points of disagreement.

Banda Singh Bahadur was commissioned by Guru Gobind Singh at Nanded in 1708 and sent north with five men and written orders.

Sirhind fell in 1710 and Wazir Khan was killed. The chronology of mobilisation should be described from its sources without treating a rhetorical nineteen-month interval as a universally established calculation.

The short-lived rule had administrative and material expressions and is associated with cultivator interests. The precise scale of agrarian change requires evidence for specific places and measures.

Its social significance should not be supported by an unsupported comparison asserting that no comparable land reform occurred anywhere for two centuries. Explain the particular policy and its limits first.

He was besieged for eight months, captured in 1715, and executed at Delhi in 1716 with his son killed in front of him.

ph10-3-building-a-state.html:
Building a State

In twenty years he went from one city to an empire running from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej and from Kashmir to the Sindh desert. Then he had to govern it, which is the harder problem and the one he is less often given credit for.

3.1 — The conquests

The expansion followed a clear logic: absorb the other misls first, then take the surrounding regions the Afghans could no longer hold.

Look at where Peshawar is.

The north-western frontier had a long history of invasions, trade and political movement. Holding Peshawar changed the strategic position in the nineteenth century. It did not literally end all movement, conflict or invasion through the wider region for all future time.

The expansion shifted the frontier and the balance of power. That is the claim to examine, rather than a dramatic assertion that traffic stopped after thousands of uninterrupted years.

The Peshawar frontier involved garrisons, campaigns and coercive administration. It was a significant achievement with continuing costs, not a permanently sealed door that removed every strategic problem.

The strategic achievement can be described on its own evidence. Ranking it as the single largest achievement across all of Punjab's history would require a different and much broader argument.

3.2 — How it was governed

The administration made use of inherited revenue and record-keeping practices. Continuity in machinery is common in state-building; it does not mean that nothing changed from the eleventh century onwards.

The language of government was Persian. The revenue system, the record-keeping and the official vocabulary were inherited from Mughal practice — because that was the working machinery available, and the earlier Punjab history explained why conquerors keep the machinery.

The territory was divided into four large provinces, each under a governor, subdivided into districts under officials called kardars who collected revenue and administered justice.

Revenue was the main business of the state, taken as a share of the crop, in kind or in cash, and often collected through contractors who bid for the right.

3.3 — Who ran it

The composition of his government is the most-cited fact about him, and it is worth being precise.

  • Fakir Azizuddin, a Muslim, was his foreign minister for decades and his most trusted envoy — the man he sent to negotiate with the British.
  • Diwan Dina Nath, a Hindu, ran the finances.
  • The Dogra brothers from Jammu — Dhian Singh as chief minister, Gulab Singh in Jammu, Suchet Singh — held enormous power. All three are Hindu Rajputs, and Chapters 7 to 9 turn on what they did with that power.
  • His generals included Sikhs, Muslims, Hindus and Europeans.

He made grants to mosques, temples and gurdwaras alike. He never levied the jizya. He funded the gold plating and marble work that gave the Harmandir Sahib the appearance it has today, and he also endowed Muslim and Hindu institutions.

3.4 — And the parts that are less comfortable

An honest account has to include these.

Sada Kaur. The mother-in-law whose alliance made his rise possible was, in 1821, stripped of her territories and held in confinement until her death. Her misl was absorbed.

The Badshahi Mosque. Lahore's great Mughal mosque was used by his army as a magazine and its precincts for stabling. Some other mosques in the city were similarly put to state use during his reign.

The misls. The confederacies of Part 9 were dismantled. Some chiefs were pensioned or given service; others lost everything.

Genuinely, and unusually for its time

Officials of different religions held substantial positions, and patronage reached varied institutions. That supports a description of a diverse court. The absence of a particular reported revolt is not proof that no subject experienced religious exclusion or coercion.

Pragmatic, and with real costs

Governing a diverse population created strong practical reasons for inclusion. Those reasons can coexist with principles and personal decisions. Neither necessity nor virtue should be asserted as the single proved private motive of the whole government.

The expansion included Amritsar, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar, with different dates and forms of control. Many Misl interests were absorbed. The statement should not erase every continuing local autonomy by saying that every other Misl was identically abolished.

Holding the frontier altered the kingdom's strategic position. It required continued resources and coercion. Its importance does not depend on a claim that every future invasion or conflict had ended permanently.

The state was run in Persian, on inherited Mughal machinery, through provinces and district officials.

His foreign minister was Muslim, his finance minister Hindu, his chief minister a Dogra Rajput. No jizya was ever levied.

And he confined the mother-in-law who made his rise possible, used the Badshahi Mosque as a magazine, and governed Kashmir and Peshawar hard. All of that is in the record too.

ph10-4-the-army.html:
The Army

Ranjit Singh developed regular forces, artillery and training while also retaining other military formations. European officers contributed to that development. The army deserves examination through organisation, equipment and costs rather than a claim that all British observers ranked it identically as Asia's most dangerous.

4.1 — Why he built it

Misl forces included mobile cavalry well suited to particular forms of conflict. Calling them unbeatable would erase real defeats and changes in conditions. Mobility was a strength, not immunity from every opponent.

Regular infantry, artillery, siege resources and drill offered capacities different from mobile cavalry. Earlier forces were not literally incapable of taking any fortified position. The issue is how a growing state developed a broader military organisation.

There is a specific moment when this became obvious to him. In 1809, during the negotiations of Chapter 5, a small British escort — a few hundred sepoys — was attacked at Amritsar by a much larger body of Sikh irregulars. The sepoys formed up, held, and drove them off with heavy losses.

Accounts of encounters with drilled troops help illustrate the value of coordinated formations. Claiming to know the ruler's exact private thought at one scene is stronger than the evidence of subsequent military development.

Training can change an engagement's result without proving that the defeated soldiers were biologically braver or inherently better horsemen. An explanation of coordination is stronger when it does not add an unmeasured hierarchy of personal worth.

Drill can coordinate loading, movement and endurance under fire. It does not make individual competence irrelevant, and its value depends on equipment, command and circumstances.

Rulers in different parts of South Asia adopted and adapted military techniques. This chapter does not establish that almost everyone except Ranjit Singh refused to learn. His development can be studied without dismissing every contemporary reform.

Ranjit Singh spent the next thirty years doing exactly that.

4.2 — The Europeans

From the early 1820s he began recruiting European officers — mostly Frenchmen and Italians, many of them veterans of Napoleon's armies who had been unemployed since 1815 and had made their way east looking for work.

The best known are Jean-Baptiste Ventura, who organised the infantry, Jean-François Allard, who built the cavalry, Claude Auguste Court, who developed the artillery, and Paolo Avitabile, who ended up as the formidable governor of Peshawar.

Their terms of service are worth reading, because they say a great deal about the man who set them.

Accounts describe conditions and expectations imposed on European officers. These varied with individuals and service arrangements; a uniform list should not be treated as a surviving identical contract for every officer. Their appointments demonstrate the ruler's use of outside expertise within his own forces.

Look at what those conditions are actually doing.

He wanted European military technique. He did not want a European enclave inside his army.

Conditions imposed on foreign officers can reflect concerns about loyalty, adaptation and service. Specific terms require the relevant contract or account. The chapter should not infer that every condition had one exclusive purpose or operated identically for every officer.

Foreign military expertise can create questions about dependence. In this case, appointments operated within the ruler's own administration. A comparison with other states needs identified examples rather than a sweeping claim that advisers routinely guaranteed foreign takeover.

The ruler drew on external expertise while maintaining his own political authority. That is an important feature, though no military organisation is entirely free of dependence on people, supplies and changing circumstances.

4.3 — What it became

Estimates of military strength vary with date and with whether they include regulars, irregulars, contingents and other formations. A total must define those categories. The earlier figure of seventy to ninety thousand should not be repeated as a securely established count of regular troops alone.

Alongside it were the irregular cavalry, the levies of his chiefs, and the Nihangs — the standing armed order from Part 9, who fought in their own way and were not drilled by anyone.

British observers took the army seriously, but their judgments should be read individually. A claim that it was the only army in India capable of facing the Company, supported unanimously by every private assessment, exceeds the material supplied here.

4.4 — What it cost

A standing army can be an achievement and a political vulnerability. The later crisis had several causes, including succession, factional conflict, resources and external intervention. The army's organisation is part of the explanation, not the sole thing that destroyed the state.

The assumption is that a strong army makes a state strong.

Only if the state can control it. A modern standing army is different in kind from a feudal levy, and the difference is not size — it is that it must be paid, continuously, in cash, whether or not there is a war.

Several practical consequences follow from keeping substantial permanent forces. They are possible pressures to investigate, not a law that every state experiences in exactly the same way.

One: it dominates the budget. A large share of the revenue of the whole empire went to the army. That means constant pressure to raise revenue, which means harder taxation, which means Chapter 6's Kashmir.

Arrears and uncertain authority can create serious instability. An army does not have to be continually used in war to justify its existence; defence, deterrence and maintained discipline also matter.

An organised armed body can acquire political leverage when authority and payment are uncertain. Other institutions and factions also remained. Calling it the only coherent institution left would hide their roles.

The army became an important political actor during the succession crisis. Explaining particular interventions requires the actors, dates and sources, rather than treating every later event as the inevitable completion of one mechanism.

Mobile cavalry and regular formations supplied different capacities. Encounters with drilled forces illustrated problems of coordination. The lesson does not depend on declaring the earlier formations incapable of every siege or engagement.

From the 1820s he hired Napoleonic veterans — Ventura, Allard, Court, Avitabile — to rebuild the army on European lines.

Foreign officers served within conditions shaped by the ruler and their circumstances. Broad summaries of those conditions require care; they do not alone establish a complete refusal of every dependency.

Strength estimates require defined categories and dates. The developing army included regular and other forces, with substantial artillery. No exact total of regulars is asserted in this adapted reading.

Permanent forces require resources and accountable command. During a succession crisis, payment and collective military interests can become politically important. That pressure was one factor among several in the kingdom's later instability.

ph11-6-counting-printing-sorting.html:
Counting, Printing, Sorting

Colonial enumeration, print and reform organisations affected the expression and political use of religious identity. That is a history of change within already existing communities and distinctions, not proof that boundaries or identification had been absent for eight hundred years.

6.1 — What identity had been like

Religious practice could overlap across sites and households, while communities also maintained real distinctions. A shared shrine or custom is evidence of interaction. It is not proof that nobody previously identified with a particular religion.

Some households participated in several local traditions. Others maintained more exclusive commitments. The diversity of practice should be preserved rather than presented as a uniform condition experienced by every village.

Overlap and identification can coexist. The question is how particular forms of official classification and community organisation altered their relationship, not whether people had previously been unable to distinguish anything.

6.2 — The census

From 1881 the British conducted a decennial census of all India. It recorded, among much else, religion.

Census categories can require a simplified recorded answer. The classification does not necessarily represent every activity or attachment in a person's life. Comparing forms and instructions across dates is necessary before treating every census as identical.

Think about what a census actually does, beyond counting.

Enumeration gives an administrative form to identity. Some people already had a clear identification; others presented harder cases. The change is in how the state records and uses the classification, not a universal first experience of choosing a religion.

Published totals increased the availability of comparisons across districts and categories. Earlier counts and classifications also existed. The modern census should not be called the first occasion on which anyone could ever know a community's size.

It makes numbers politically valuable. Once representation, jobs and grants start being distributed by community — which they increasingly were — the size of your community becomes an asset.

Where numbers affect representation or resources, organisations can have incentives to define membership and attract declarations of affiliation. The response varies by group and circumstance; it should not be described as an automatic identical change in every organisation.

This identifies a mechanism that can operate without one secret plan. It does not rule out deliberate policies or prove the private intentions of every administrator. Particular decisions still need their records.

6.3 — The reform movements

Into this arrived the printing press, cheap vernacular publishing, the railway, and a generation of educated men with a reforming temperament. The result was a wave of organisations across all three communities, and they defined themselves against each other.

The Arya Samaj, founded by Dayanand Saraswati in 1875 and established at Lahore in 1877, became powerful in Punjab. It called for a return to the Vedas, rejected idol worship and priestly authority, campaigned against caste discrimination and for women's education — and, decisively, developed shuddhi, a rite for bringing converts and their descendants back into the Hindu fold.

The Singh Sabha movement began at Amritsar in 1873 and Lahore in 1879. It aimed to reform Sikh practice, promote education and Punjabi in Gurmukhi, and — increasingly, in its Lahore wing — to define Sikh identity as distinct rather than as a branch of Hinduism. Khalsa College was founded at Amritsar in 1892. In 1898 a leading Singh Sabha writer published a book whose title translates as "We Are Not Hindus". The Anand Marriage Act of 1909 gave the Sikh marriage rite legal standing of its own.

Muslim organisations developed in parallel — the Anjuman-i-Himayat-i-Islam at Lahore in 1884, Islamia College, a large publishing effort, and reform currents arriving from the seminaries of northern India. The Ahmadiyya movement was founded at Qadian in Punjab in 1889 and became a source of intense controversy in its own right.

Largely yes — it was made by colonial machinery

Official classifications, electoral arrangements and recruitment practices could sharpen the political value of identity. They operated on communities with older histories and boundaries. Saying there had been no prior boundaries would erase that history.

No — the material was already there

The earlier history contains real religious distinctions, commitments and persecution as well as overlap. Reformers also acted for their own reasons. A colonial explanation should recognise that agency while examining the state's effects.

Underneath the whole argument sits a belief that feels self-evident:

The assumption is that measuring something does not change it.

A census sounds like a photograph. It is not. It is an instrument that acts on what it measures.

Classification can influence what it describes, especially when benefits or restrictions attach to categories. The effect is not necessarily automatic or identical everywhere. A careful account examines the instructions, the actual responses and the consequences.

  • Ambiguity is destroyed. People who lived between categories must now be assigned.
  • The categories acquire boundaries. Someone must decide the edge cases, and deciding an edge case is defining a boundary.
  • The count becomes a resource. And anything that is a resource will be competed for.

Recruitment and electoral categories are related examples of classification affecting opportunity. Each has its own history. Their existence does not establish a single inevitable pathway to the violence of 1947.

A mechanism can matter alongside deliberate policy. The absence of a single demonstrated master plan is not proof that nobody pursued divisive aims, and the existence of an official category is not proof of an intention to cause every later conflict.

Local overlap existed alongside religious identity before the colonial census. The census changed how affiliation was recorded and made some comparisons more politically useful; it did not invent all membership or every boundary.

The census from 1881 required exactly that, published the totals, and — as benefits came to be distributed by community — made the numbers worth fighting over.

Reform movements rose across all three communities and defined themselves against each other: the Arya Samaj, the Singh Sabha, and Muslim organisations at Lahore.

Existing communities changed under enumeration, reform, print and political competition. Their boundaries were neither wholly absent earlier nor perfectly uniform later. The transformation is worth explaining without a slogan that deletes one half of the history.

Measuring something is not photographing it. A census acts on what it counts.

ph12-5-the-akali-decade.html:
The Akali Decade

The Gurdwara Reform movement combined religious concerns, institutional control and political organisation. Its campaigns had lasting consequences. They were not simply an apolitical dispute that accidentally became political, because control, law and authority were already involved.

The movement concerned the administration and conduct of significant gurdwaras. Religious principles, property arrangements and colonial authority were connected questions from the beginning, even when participants emphasised particular grievances.

Mahants managed various shrines and endowments under differing arrangements. Reformers criticised abuses, exclusion and control by particular custodians. It would be inaccurate to make every mahant a hereditary proprietor with exactly the same conduct or legal position.

A gurdwara is a Sikh place of worship. The word means "door of the Guru".

Colonial recognition of existing managers could bring reformers into conflict with state authority. The legal arrangements varied. A dispute about a shrine was not automatically identical to an attack on the government in every instance.

A conflict over custody and property could involve state power. The reformers also had religious and political aims. Law contributed to the setting; it did not alone predetermine every action or leave participants without choices.

Two organisations in one month

In November 1920 a representative body was formed to manage the shrines: the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, or SGPC. In December 1920 a second body was formed to supply the volunteers who would take the shrines: the Shiromani Akali Dal.

Akali means a follower of Akal, the Timeless One — God. The name was borrowed from an older warrior tradition.

A jatha is a band or a squad — a group of volunteers sent to do something together.

A morcha is a front, in the military sense; in Punjabi political usage it means a sustained campaign of confrontation over one issue.

The method was Gandhian in form and Sikh in discipline. A jatha would march to a shrine, unarmed, take an oath not to strike back, and present itself. It would be beaten, arrested, or both. The next jatha would arrive the following day. Then the next.

Nankana Sahib

On 20 February 1921 a jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh entered the gurdwara at Nankana Sahib — the birthplace of Guru Nanak. The mahant, Narain Das, had hired armed men in anticipation. The gates were shut and the jatha was killed inside the compound. Contemporary accounts put the dead at around 130. Bodies were burned.

Around 130 unarmed men, who had taken an oath not to resist, killed in the compound of the shrine marking the birthplace of the founder of their faith.

The killing at Nankana Sahib in February 1921 gave a powerful impetus to reform. Its impact belongs beside the organising work already under way. Calling one morning the whole explanation for the movement's subsequent success would erase the campaigns and institutions that followed.

Two further campaigns defined the decade. At Guru ka Bagh, near Amritsar, in 1922, jathas were beaten systematically by police over several months while crowds watched and Indian and foreign observers reported it. At Jaito, in the princely state of Nabha, a morcha begun in 1923 ran for years, and a jatha marching there was fired on in February 1924.

Reports, testimony and organisational records contribute to the history of the morchas. Public visibility mattered to the campaigns, but the record's existence should not be explained exclusively by one deliberate publicity strategy.

The SGPC kept lists — of jathas sent, of men arrested, of men injured, of money collected. It invited journalists. At Guru ka Bagh the beatings were witnessed by reporters and by the English clergyman C. F. Andrews, whose published account caused an uproar.

This was strategy, not luck. A movement whose entire method is being beaten without hitting back needs the beating to be seen. The record exists because being on the record was the weapon.

The Act, and what it built

The 1925 Act provided an institutional settlement for specified gurdwaras. The SGPC's jurisdiction and electoral arrangements must be described through the statute, not projected as a universal authority over every Sikh institution worldwide.

The movement had won what it asked for. It had also, without quite intending to, created something new.

The SGPC controlled the great shrines. The shrines had enormous incomes from offerings. The SGPC was filled by elections on a Sikh electoral roll. And standing beside it was the Akali Dal, a party with a proven ability to put thousands of disciplined volunteers on the road at short notice.

The case that it was

A favourable assessment can recognise campaigns for community control, disciplined protest and institutional reform. The same history contains costs and contested decisions. Neither the success nor the criticism should be framed through a claim that no other movement achieved anything comparable.

The case that it was costly

A critical assessment asks how religious institutions, resources and party politics became linked. That is a question about particular arrangements and consequences, not proof that every subsequent Sikh political choice was determined by one machine.

Both the reformers and the government assumed the question "who is a Sikh?" had a clear answer, because the Act required one. To hold elections you need a roll. To make a roll you need a definition.

The Act required definitions and procedures for its electoral arrangements. Punjabi religious life contained both clear identities and overlapping practices. Legal boundaries did not create all identity from nothing, even though their administration could sharpen particular distinctions.

The statutory classification addressed an institutional purpose. It could also influence later debates. The exact consequences need evidence about people and organisations, not a universal claim that every category was simply a convenience that later became reality.

The movement challenged particular custodial arrangements and abuses. Legal protection of incumbents brought state authority into the disputes. The managers and institutions were not identical, so their replacement should not be described as one uniform transfer from hereditary ownership everywhere.

Nonviolent mobilisation was important in the reform campaigns. Its role can be described without asserting that every volunteer, locality or event followed an identical sequence.

The SGPC and Akali Dal became significant institutions with distinct responsibilities and later histories. Their relationship deserves study without assuming that every political calculation for two decades reduced to one fixed combination.

ph13-2-the-killing.html:
The Killing

There is no agreed exhaustive count of Partition deaths. Records and estimates exist, but their scope and methods differ. Saying nobody counted would erase real documentation while obscuring the limits that make a precise final total difficult.

2.1 — It did not start in August#

Large-scale violence in Punjab preceded the August border announcements. The March 1947 violence in the Rawalpindi region is important to the sequence. Earlier communal violence elsewhere also belongs to the wider history; March should not be declared the first violence anywhere in the subcontinent.

That earlier round matters for understanding what came later. Refugees from Rawalpindi arrived in central and eastern Punjab through the spring, carrying accounts of what had been done to their villages. Some of them were among the men who organised what happened in August, in the other direction.

Displacement and accounts of attacks could contribute to retaliatory mobilisation. That mechanism helps explain some events. It does not establish that every refugee participated in violence or that every later attack had the same cause.

2.2 — It was organised#

The common phrase is that Punjab "descended into madness". The evidence does not support the picture that phrase creates.

The records include organised armed attacks, alongside varied local circumstances. Leaders, training and transport matter where documented. A claim about planning should name the actor or incident rather than turn every violent event into one uniform coordinated operation.

They attacked minority settlements, usually at a numerical advantage of many to one. They frequently attacked at the moment a community was most exposed: a village whose men had left, a column on the road, a train.

Jatha means a band or group and appears in different settings, including nonviolent protest and armed mobilisation. A shared word does not establish identical aims, membership or moral justification.

Vocabulary can connect movements in memory. The word alone does not prove how every participant justified an action. Motives and continuities need their own evidence.

Three kinds of evidence, none complete.

Official reports and administrative records can establish events and contemporary perceptions. Breakdowns and institutional interests affect them. A claim that both new governments deliberately reduced every figure would require specific evidence beyond the record's incompleteness.

Relief: registers from refugee camps and from the Military Evacuation Organisation, recording arrivals, deaths in camp, and people reported missing.

Survivor accounts contribute detailed local experiences. Their timing, memory and scope must be considered. They should not be dismissed as universally unreliable, but neither can an individual witness supply an exhaustive total for a whole region.

Different kinds of evidence support the occurrence of large-scale violence and displacement. They have different coverage and limitations. Their agreement about particular patterns does not make any one record a complete list of everyone killed.

2.3 — The trains#

Trains carried refugees in both directions. They were also the easiest targets in Punjab: a known route, a fixed timetable, hundreds of people packed in with nowhere to go.

Trains were vulnerable targets and attacks contributed to fear and retaliation. The record supports their importance without proving that no village attack ever caused comparable losses.

2.4 — What happened to women#

A large part of the violence was directed specifically at women, and it needs to be described rather than gestured at.

Women were abducted in very large numbers, and were killed by attackers. Women were also killed by their own families, and killed themselves, to avoid capture — a fact recorded on all sides, and one that families themselves recounted afterwards as honourable.

Women faced abduction, sexual violence, killing and coercion, including within their own communities. The post-Partition recovery arrangements also created difficult questions about consent and belonging. Exact totals require a defined administrative record; no precise count of all affected women is asserted here.

A working estimate made for recovery is not an exhaustive count of every abduction. It can still reveal scale if its categories and period are identified. Figures should not be moved between countries, provinces and kinds of harm as though their definitions were identical.

The recovery operation ran for years. It also took women back from households where they had since had children, sometimes against their stated wishes — so it produced a second displacement of its own.

Both governments treated recovery as obviously right, and both used the same reasoning: a woman taken from one community belonged with that community, and returning her restored something.

The assumption underneath is that a woman's community membership is a fact about her that cannot change, and that her own statement about where she wished to live could be overridden by it.

Recovery laws and practices should be read in their actual wording and application. Questions of age, sex, community identification and consent require that text, not a compressed universal assertion about every person handled by the programme.

I am not telling you the recovery operation was wrong. Many women were being held by force and wanted out. I am pointing at the premise that made it possible not to ask.

2.5 — The number nobody has#

Published death estimates vary widely and often concern different geographical scopes. Estimates for all of Partition must not automatically be relabelled as estimates for Punjab alone. A comparison needs the same territory, time span and categories.

The case for the lower figures

Document-based estimates can miss deaths where records broke down. That limitation is important. It does not mean every lower estimate uses exactly the same method or that the source boundaries can be ignored.

The case for the higher figures

Demographic estimates depend on assumptions about migration, missing people and population change. Those assumptions need inspection. A high estimate should not be presented as an exact count merely because it comes from a calculation.

The middle position

The responsible formulation is a range or clearly attributed estimate with its scope attached. A single precise total may suggest a completeness the evidence does not have. Uncertainty in the total does not erase documented events or individual victims.

Punjab's large-scale violence before and during Partition occurred in waves with different local histories. Displacement and retaliation mattered, alongside organised mobilisation and failures of protection.

Organised attacks are documented in particular settings. Responsibility belongs to named actors and events rather than every member of a religious community.

The violence against women and the later recovery arrangements require attention to coercion and consent. Their experiences should not be reduced to symbols of a community's honour.

No exhaustive agreed death total is supplied here. Actual counts and estimates have differing limits. The gap does not prove a single intentional concealment by all governments; the conduct of particular institutions requires its own evidence.

ph13-8-the-decade-that-is-still-being-ar.html:
The Decade That Is Still Being Argued About

This adapted background separates chronology from assessments of responsibility. It is read alongside the dated inquiry, judicial and human-rights records linked in Part 11, rather than used as a new independent witness.

8.1 — How I am going to do this#

The events remain part of living memory for survivors and families. That makes care with language important. It does not justify assuming that every participant mentioned in an earlier account is still alive at this edition's date.

Describe the sequence, identify the source for a figure and distinguish findings from allegations. These are practical obligations. A disagreement should be explained in prose, with the relevant evidence beside it.

The chapter does make ethical judgments against killings of civilians and violations of rights. It does not pretend that those judgments establish every factual allegation. Responsibility should be named at the level the available evidence supports.

8.2 — What was being demanded#

The Anandpur Sahib Resolution dates to 1973, with later revisions and political uses. Claims about its demands require an identified version. Saying that almost nobody has read it is not evidence about its text or its readership.

Its contents, in plain terms: more powers for states and fewer for the centre, with the centre restricted to defence, foreign affairs, currency and communications; Chandigarh transferred to Punjab; the Punjabi-speaking areas left out in 1966 transferred in; a larger share of river water; a higher share of army recruitment; and recognition of Sikhism's distinct status, including a demand that it not be treated as a branch of Hinduism in law.

This is a dispute about a text, which makes it unusually tractable — and it was never resolved anyway.

Read as a federal demand

On this reading it is a demand for genuine federalism, of a kind argued for by regional parties in Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and elsewhere. It nowhere asks for a separate country. Its language about state powers closely tracks mainstream federalist argument of the period. Several later commissions on centre-state relations took up similar themes. Read plainly, it is a bargaining document about autonomy.

Read as a separatist demand

Some opponents read its demands as approaching separation in practice. That interpretation must be distinguished from an explicit demand for independence and from the later positions of particular militant actors. A political reading is not a substitute for the wording of an identified version.

8.3 — The sequence#

In 1982 the Akali Dal launched the Dharam Yudh Morcha, a mass civil-disobedience campaign in the pattern described in Part 12 — jathas courting arrest, in very large numbers.

Alongside it, a separate and increasingly armed current developed, associated with the preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale. Targeted killings began. Through 1983 the state's authority eroded. President's rule was imposed in October 1983.

Bhindranwale and armed followers took up residence in the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar, fortifying buildings inside it, including the Akal Takht.

Akal Takht: "throne of the Timeless One", the seat of temporal authority in Sikhism, founded by Guru Hargobind and described in Part 8. It faces the Harmandir Sahib — the Golden Temple — across the pool.

Its meaning is why what happened there is not comparable to a siege of an ordinary building. It is the institution from which the community's collective decisions are announced.

In June 1984 the Indian Army was sent in. Operation Blue Star ran from 1 to 8 June. It used tanks. Bhindranwale was killed. The Akal Takht was extensively destroyed.

The operation took place in the first week of June, when the complex was crowded with pilgrims for the martyrdom anniversary of Guru Arjan.

The official account

Official and other casualty figures for June differ. The evidence consulted here does not establish one exhaustive independently verified count. A precise official figure and its categories should be quoted from the actual report, not used without that address.

The higher estimates

Higher estimates have been offered with criticisms of access and counting. The criticism is relevant, but each estimate still needs its own method and scope. An unverified high figure does not become exact merely because an official tally is contested.

On 31 October 1984 Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two of her bodyguards, both Sikhs.

In the days that followed, organised mobs attacked Sikhs, above all in Delhi but also in other cities. Households were identified, often from electoral rolls. Men were killed in the street and burned. Official figures put the Delhi dead at around 2,700; other counts run higher, and there were further deaths elsewhere.

November 1984 is documented far better than June 1984, and the difference is instructive.

The Nanavati Commission provides a detailed dated inquiry record for the November violence. Its testimony and findings should be distinguished. Other reports exist; counting inquiries does not itself establish independence or agreement about every allegation.

The report found organised violence and serious failures of police protection, while setting limits on findings about direction from the highest level. Those limits must be included alongside the findings about local actors and institutional failure.

Delayed proceedings and unresolved grievances are important. A concrete dated result is the Delhi High Court's 17 December 2018 conviction involving Sajjan Kumar. It should not be erased by saying nothing has been adjudicated, or expanded into a claim that every case is resolved.

In ordinary discussion, riot can suggest disorder, but legal rioting can involve organised action. The word does not inherently prove spontaneity. Describing documented planning is more informative than assuming that one label settles the question.

Different labels can emphasise different aspects of an event. The reader should see the underlying acts and findings. June and November had different actors and processes and should not be collapsed into one undifferentiated episode.

The evidence in November 1984 shows lists, transport, fuel and a pattern of police inaction. Those are the marks of organisation, not of frenzy. Many Sikh organisations therefore use the word pogrom, and several Indian courts have since used language closer to organised violence than to rioting.

Use a label with its meaning explained and the evidence visible. Pogrom can communicate targeted violence; genocide has a particular legal definition. Neither word should be converted into a criminal conviction that the cited judgment did not make.

8.4 — The years after#

An accord was signed in July 1985 between Rajiv Gandhi and the Akali leader Harchand Singh Longowal, promising Chandigarh to Punjab and referring the other disputes to commissions. Longowal was assassinated the following month. Chandigarh was not transferred.

What followed was roughly a decade of armed militancy and counter-insurgency. Militant groups killed civilians, officials and each other; bus massacres and bombings killed large numbers of ordinary Punjabis of every community. The state responded with emergency laws, mass detention, and a police campaign that became notorious for extrajudicial killings and disappearances.

Jaswant Singh Khalra's work drew attention to police cremation records. The subsequent official proceedings provide a defined evidence trail. His role matters, alongside the investigators, records and institutions through which findings were reached.

The NHRC proceedings covered cremations at three identified crematoria, with categories concerning identification, custody and the dignity of remains. These findings should be described from the record rather than turned into proof that every body in one aggregate total was murdered.

The defined scope cannot simply be multiplied into a statewide total. Other allegations require their own evidence. A limited official proceeding can establish serious violations without establishing the full scale of every other allegation.

Elections and a decline in violence changed the political setting during the 1990s. An election does not prove that every fear, abuse or unresolved case ended. Claims about exact turnout and participation need their own electoral records.

It was defeated by the police

One explanation emphasises policing and the disruption of militant organisations. That explanation does not establish that unlawful methods were necessary or justified in every case. The means used remain answerable to evidence and law.

It lost its people

Another explanation emphasises declining support and harms inflicted by militant groups. Such claims need attention to locality and period. They should not be turned into an unmeasured assertion about what every Punjabi privately believed.

Both, plus exhaustion

Exhaustion can also matter, but an analyst should not infer universal consent to abuse from a desire for violence to end. A population can want security and still have claims against those providing it.

Federal autonomy, statehood and independence are distinct demands. The resolution's identified text and later actors' uses of it require separate discussion rather than a single permanent label.

June involved a military assault at a major sacred complex and severe destruction and deaths. The uncertainty of the exhaustive casualty total should remain attached to figures, not be used to erase civilians or to invent an exact replacement.

November involved targeted anti-Sikh killings and failures of protection documented in inquiries and court records. The findings should be read in their actual scope, including limits and particular named judicial results.

Later violence includes crimes by militant groups and allegations and findings concerning state actors. The NHRC cremation proceedings have defined categories; they are not an all-purpose statewide register of every death.

Some important matters have been examined by inquiries, commissions and courts; others remain unresolved or contested. Saying almost nothing has been settled would erase those findings. Saying everything has been resolved would erase the limits.
